role.altitude: The applicator keeps inspecting plants, diagnosing problems, deciding treatment, adjusting routes to weather and signalling drivers on site; writing up spray books, updating stock lists, ordering stops on a map and looking up symptoms in printed guides shrink.
skills_to_grow: Using the spray record app and sprayer GPS logs
role.ambitious_version: An applicator whose records are complete when the sprayer stops, and who spends the saved time checking sites and weather.

tasks.short: Record the product, authorisation number and dose, record location, area and timing, update stock, check the final record, and send it to the client to record information about pesticide applications.

steps.what: Applicator records the pesticide type used, authorisation number and dose: in the spray book today; after the change picks the product from the register list, which fills the authorisation number and allowed dose, and enters the dose used

Applicator records location, area treated, amount applied, date and time: by hand today; after the change the sprayer's GPS log fills them for about 70% of applications and the applicator checks them, while handheld work is still entered by hand
Applicator updates the product stock list
Applicator checks the final application record: product, dose, location, area and times against what was done
Applicator sends the application record to the client

tasks.design: A spray record app replaces the paper spray book. The applicator picks the product from a list fed by the authorisation register, which fills the authorisation number and allowed dose. The sprayer's GPS log fills location, area treated and times. Stock updates from suppliers' electronic delivery notes and the recorded use. The applicator checks the completed record and sends that version to the client as a machine-readable export instead of copies by mail. GPS logs are used for the records only; any other use is agreed with the works council first.
tasks.previous_blocker: Paper spray books and spreadsheets mailed to clients.
tasks.enabler_now: Spray record apps with product registers, supplier messages and sprayer GPS.
tasks.human_edge: Noting the drift risk the wind created on the day.

reach.learn: Whether records are complete at inspection.

evidence.claim: A Dutch farm software keeps spray registrations and updates stock from suppliers' electronic delivery notes.
From 2026 records of plant protection product use must be machine-readable and electronic.
Sprayer GPS that shows who sprayed where can monitor workers and needs works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: recording applications; the Dutch ban on most professional use outside agriculture keeps volume small.
Input contract for s2: sprayers with GPS logging, about 70% of applications; handheld work is entered by hand; s2 is priced at that share.

Checking keeps its full time. s1 keeps 50 because the register fills product details and the applicator still enters the dose used. s2 keeps 45: about 30% handheld work typed in full plus a check of the GPS-filled fields. s3 keeps 20 for checking the stock list. s5 keeps 40 for the export and answering the client's questions about it.
research_questions: Are records complete at inspection more often?

incremental.description: Applicator checks GPS logs and product lists for errors.

approvals.approved_version: The application record with product, authorisation number, dose, location, area and times exactly as checked by the applicator in s4, sent once as an export to the client of that site; any change needs a new check before sending.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: much handheld spraying, so only about 30% of applications have a GPS log, and some suppliers send no electronic delivery notes; s2 keeps 75 and s3 keeps 50 (35.5); high: GPS on about 70% as assumed (49.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Review sites and timing windows, order the stops to establish driving routes for pesticide applications, adjust the route to weather and access, and brief the driver.

steps.what: Applicator reviews treatment sites, timing windows and restrictions
Applicator orders the stops to establish the driving route
Applicator adjusts the route for weather and site access on the day
Applicator briefs the driver on the route

tasks.design: Sites appear on a map in the planning tool with their timing windows and restrictions such as buffer zones, instead of a pile of work orders. A route planner orders the stops by distance and time window. Adjusting for wind, rain and access on the day, and briefing the driver, stay with the applicator.
tasks.previous_blocker: Routes were worked out on paper maps.
tasks.enabler_now: Route planners with time windows and site maps.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which site will be too windy by afternoon.
tasks.altitude: Less route planning; weather judgement stays.

evidence.claim: Route planners order stops by distance and time windows.

assumptions: Boundary: planning routes; recording applications (task 24043) is a sibling task.
Input contract for s1: site locations and restrictions entered in the planning tool by the office.
Adjusting and briefing keep their full time.
research_questions: Does driving distance per day fall?

incremental.description: Applicator corrects site locations and access notes.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few sites per day with fixed access times, so the planner's order is often redone by hand and s2 keeps 70 (17.5); high: the planner's order is used (28.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Inspect plants and lawns, look up symptoms, identify lawn or plant diseases to determine the appropriate course of treatment, and explain it to the client.

steps.what: Applicator inspects plants and lawns on site
Applicator looks up the symptoms in reference guides

loop.input: Photos of the affected plants or lawn.
loop.output: Likely diseases or pests with links to reference pages.
loop.check: The applicator compares each suggestion with the reference description and the symptoms seen on site; a suggestion that does not match what they see is dropped, and unclear cases go to the printed guide or a plant health adviser.
loop.stop: No good match: the applicator uses the printed guide or sends a sample to a lab.
loop.why_not_simpler: Symptoms look alike and vary by plant.

steps.what: Applicator identifies the disease and determines the appropriate course of treatment
Applicator explains the diagnosis and treatment to the client

tasks.design: A photo identification app suggests likely diseases or pests with links to reference pages, which the applicator compares with what they see, instead of leafing through a printed guide. Inspecting, diagnosing, choosing treatment (non-chemical first where rules require) and explaining stay with the applicator.
tasks.previous_blocker: Symptoms were looked up in printed guides.
tasks.enabler_now: Photo identification apps for plant diseases.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that the real problem is drainage, not disease.

reach.learn: Whether treatments work first time more often.

evidence.claim: Photo identification apps suggest plant diseases with reference pages.
Professional use of pesticides outside agriculture in the Netherlands is banned with exceptions.

assumptions: Boundary: identifying diseases and choosing treatment; recording applications (task 24043) is a sibling task.
Inspecting, diagnosing and explaining keep their full time.
unknowns: How often the applicator needs to look up symptoms.

incremental.description: Applicator falls back to the printed guide when the app's suggestions do not fit what is seen.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly familiar problems or plants the app does not know, so the guide is still used and s2 keeps 85 (2.8); high: the app gives fitting suggestions (7.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Agree signals and route with the driver, provide driving instructions using hand and horn signals to ensure complete coverage of designated areas, and check coverage.

steps.what: Applicator agrees signals and the route with the truck driver before starting
Applicator provides driving instructions to the truck driver using hand and horn signals
Applicator checks complete coverage of the designated areas

tasks.design: A GPS guidance display in the cab shows the driver the next pass and the treated area, so the applicator signals less often and still guides at edges and obstacles. The applicator checks coverage on the treated-area map instead of only by eye. Agreeing signals stays as it is.
tasks.previous_blocker: Coverage depended on signals and visual checks alone.
tasks.enabler_now: GPS guidance displays and treated-area maps.
tasks.still_hard: Irregular areas with trees and obstacles.
tasks.human_edge: Stopping the truck before a child steps into the area.

evidence.claim: GPS guidance displays show drivers passes and treated areas.
Location systems that show who drove where need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: guiding the driver; route planning (task 24044) is a sibling task.
Input contract for s2 and s3: GPS guidance on about half of the spray trucks; s2 and s3 are priced at that share.
Agreeing signals keeps its full time.

incremental.description: Applicator checks the guidance setup at the start of each job.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: irregular areas where the applicator signals at most passes and checks by eye, so s2 keeps 95 and s3 keeps 80 (7.2); high: GPS guidance on half of trucks as assumed (14.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
